title: Nzambi and the Creation
source_ref: Kongo oral tradition; Bunseki Fu-Kiau, African Cosmology of the Bantu-Kongo (1980; English translation 2001)
paragraphs: In Kongo tradition, Nzambi Mpungu is the creator, the great spirit behind everything that exists. The name is often translated simply as God, and in Kikongo it is still used that way. Nzambi is not an abstraction in the old accounts: the world, the rivers, the forest and the ancestors all depend on the power that made them.

One widely told account says that Nzambi made the sky, the earth and the water, then set the sun and moon above them and filled the rivers with fish. The first people were shaped from earth, or came down from the sky, depending on the version. When the work was finished, the creator withdrew.

That withdrawal matters. In everyday Kongo life, people addressed ancestors, land spirits and the powers called simbi or nkisi rather than the creator directly. Nzambi was the source of life, but the dead, the fields and the households were nearer at hand. The creator could be honoured, but not approached like a local spirit with a bargain.

The story changed as it travelled. Missionaries in the Kingdom of Kongo, which adopted Christianity in the late fifteenth century, identified Nzambi with the Christian God, and that equation shaped later retellings. Bunseki Fu-Kiau, writing in the twentieth century, set Nzambi inside a Kongo cosmology of the sun's four movements, where life, death and rebirth turn in a circle.
notes: Kongo accounts differ on whether the first people were shaped from earth, came down from the sky, or were made in some other way, and some traditions name a companion, Nzambici. The identification of Nzambi with the Christian God began with mission contact in the late fifteenth century and continues in modern Kikongo usage, so the written record blends Kongo and Christian categories. Fu-Kiau's reading is a twentieth-century synthesis, not a single inherited text.

title: Mwindo
source_ref: The Mwindo epic of the Nyanga, recorded by Daniel Biebuyck and Kahombo C. Mateene from the bard Candi Rureke (1969)
paragraphs: Nyanga storytellers begin with Shemwindo, a chief who ordered his wives to bear only daughters. One wife, Nyamwindo, gave birth to a boy who refused the ordinary way into the world. Mwindo came out walking and talking, already holding his conga scepter, and announced that he was a man. His father's command had been broken by a newborn who could argue.

Shemwindo tried to kill the child. He buried him, threw him into a river and set traps, but Mwindo survived each attempt, helped by his aunt Iyangura and by his own quick tongue. The boy grew into a formidable young man and demanded his father's chiefdom. Shemwindo fled, and Mwindo followed, determined to settle the quarrel face to face.

The chase led to the underworld, the realm of Muisa. There Mwindo faced a power greater than his father and won by courage, trickery and the strength of his conga. He brought Shemwindo home and was reconciled with him. The return from the land of the dead is the heart of the epic: the hero comes back with what he went to find.

The epic is long, loud and funny. Bards perform it at night before an audience, and Mwindo's boasts, his father's panic and the underworld's absurd tests are played for laughter as well as awe. Daniel Biebuyck recorded a full version from the bard Candi Rureke and published it in 1969. The story is also about legitimate rule: Mwindo's victory establishes the chiefdom.

title: The Chameleon's Message
source_ref: Zulu and Xhosa oral tradition; southern African variants collected by Henry Callaway (1868) and later writers
paragraphs: Unkulunkulu, the old one, made people and did not mean them to die. He called the chameleon and gave it a message for the villages: tell them that people will not die. The chameleon set off slowly, as chameleons do, and stopped to eat on the way. The news was urgent, but the messenger was not.

A lizard, or in some versions a skink or a salamander, heard the errand and ran ahead. It reached the people first and told them the opposite: people will die and not return. By the time the chameleon arrived, out of breath, the people had already accepted the lizard's words. The message could not be called back.

Southern African versions disagree about almost everything except the ending. Sometimes the chameleon is slow because it stops to eat, sometimes because it is proud, and sometimes the lizard is sent deliberately with a second message. In Xhosa tellings the messengers differ, and in Kongo and East African variants other animals carry the news. The constant is that death arrives through delay.

The tale explains death without a fall from grace. No one disobeys a command and no one is punished; a message simply arrives too late. That makes the chameleon an ambiguous figure, patient and beautiful but unsuited to urgency, and the lizard a trickster or a realist depending on the teller. The story is still told across southern Africa as an answer to a child's question.
notes: Zulu and Xhosa versions name different messengers, usually a chameleon and a lizard but sometimes a skink, a salamander or another animal. The reason for the delay varies (eating, slowness, pride, deliberate trickery), and some versions have the creator send the second message himself. This retelling follows the common Zulu and Xhosa outline and keeps the ending that most versions share.

title: Mbidi Kiluwe and Kalala Ilunga
source_ref: Luba oral tradition; Thomas Q. Reefe, The Rainbow and the Kings: A History of the Luba Empire to 1891 (1981)
paragraphs: Luba tradition tells of Mbidi Kiluwe, a prince from the east who crossed the river into the land of the Luba. He was a hunter and a stranger, and he brought a new kind of rule: a king who stood apart, spoke through ritual and did not eat in public. The land already had a king, Nkongolo, whose power was older and rougher.

Mbidi was received at Nkongolo's court and stayed. He fathered a son, Kalala Ilunga, with a woman of the land. Then Mbidi returned east, crossing the water he had come from, and left the boy behind. Kalala Ilunga grew up between two claims: his father's foreign royalty and the local king's established power.

Kalala Ilunga became a rival. Nkongolo set him tests and tried to humble him; the young man passed them, and the court divided. In the end Kalala Ilunga defeated Nkongolo and took the throne. He is remembered as the first true mulopwe, the king whose line ruled the Luba and whose power was ritual as much as military.

The story is political. It explains why the Luba king rules, why he is set apart from ordinary people, and why the royal line traces back to a stranger from the east. Reciters of the Mbudye society preserved it as a charter of kingship, and Thomas Reefe read it as a foundation myth that legitimates a particular dynasty. It is history and ideology at once.

title: Kintu and Nambi
source_ref: Ganda oral tradition; John Roscoe, The Baganda (1911), with later Ganda and comparative scholarship
paragraphs: Ganda tradition tells that Kintu was the first man on earth. He kept a cow and lived alone. One day Nambi, daughter of Gulu, the lord of the sky, came down with her sister and met him. She stayed. When Gulu learned that his daughter had married a man of the earth, he summoned Kintu to heaven to answer for it.

Kintu went up. Gulu set him tests, and Kintu passed them with patience and with help from Nambi. In some tellings he had to answer riddles or prove he could provide for a household; in others the tests are barely mentioned. Gulu relented and gave the couple cattle, a goat, a sheep, a hen and banana plants.

They were warned not to come back. But something was forgotten, a seed for the hen or a piece of the bride's gear, and Kintu returned to fetch it. Walumbe, Nambi's brother, whose name means sickness, followed him down, or came with them from the start. Either way, death reached the earth with the first family.

Gulu's order and Kintu's errand explain why people die. The story also sets out a moral order: the sky is owed respect, marriage creates obligations between earth and heaven, and a small carelessness can carry a permanent cost. Missionary and colonial collectors wrote down the versions we have, and Ganda scholars have retold them ever since.
notes: Ganda versions differ on the tests Gulu sets, on what was forgotten, and on how Walumbe arrives: he may follow Kintu, be sent by Gulu, or come down with Nambi from the beginning. Some traditions identify Kintu with the first king of Buganda as well as the first man. John Roscoe's 1911 account, written for a colonial-era readership, shapes the best-known English version.

title: The Rain Queen
source_ref: Balobedu oral tradition and the living office of Modjadji; ethnographic accounts including Krige and Krige, The Realm of a Rain-Queen (1943)
paragraphs: Modjadji is the title of the rain queen of the Balobedu, a kingdom in what is now Limpopo province, South Africa. The queen is not a character from an old text. She is a living ruler, and the office has been held by a succession of women whose authority is both political and ritual. Her rain-making belongs to the land and its seasons.

Balobedu tradition holds that the queen's power over rain comes from her ancestors and from her own ritual standing. She lives at the royal village near the Modjadji cycad forest, and the community brings her tribute and asks her to intercede for rain. In good years the rain is her blessing; in drought the same belief makes her the focus of anxiety.

The office passes through women. The queen traditionally does not marry, and her successor is chosen from her daughters, so the line is traced through mothers rather than fathers. Several queens have reigned under the name Modjadji. Modjadji I is remembered as the founder of the line; Modjadji VI died in 2005, and the succession has been contested since.

Outside writers have often made the queen exotic, a hidden woman with mysterious powers. That framing says more about colonial and apartheid-era audiences than about the Balobedu. Today the queenship continues in Limpopo, and the rain queen's story belongs to a community with its own historians, protocols and arguments. It is a living institution, not a fossil.
notes: This is a living tradition, not an ancient text. The founding story, the number and names of past queens, and the rules of succession are told differently within the community and have been reshaped by colonial records, apartheid-era administration and recent disputes. The queen's ritual role is described here only in general terms; specific rites are not public, and the 1943 Krige ethnography is a dated source.
